The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect the well-known phenomenon that uncertainty scales with the square root of time. The 1-day interval of roughly plus or minus 30 points is relatively tight, reflecting the predictability of short-term price behavior under normal market conditions and assuming low intraday volatility. By the 1-week horizon, the interval widens to approximately plus or minus 67 points, accounting for the possibility of macro data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments that could shift sentiment materially. Liquidity crunches or flash crash dynamics could also push short-term prices outside even the 1-day interval in extreme cases. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic print, a dovish policy surprise, or a short squeeze in a thinly traded market could produce a rapid rally that exceeds the upper bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals assume relatively normal distributional behavior, but financial markets are known to exhibit fat tails. The true probability of extreme outcomes is likely higher than a Gaussian-based framework would suggest, meaning real-world tail risks — both to the upside and downside — are not fully captured within the stated 90% confidence intervals. Users should treat these estimates as informed central tendencies rather than precise probabilistic guarantees.
